newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japanese ministers, legislators visit war shrine.
newsitem.headline: Japanese ministers, legislators visit war shrine.

text.p: A group of 150 members of Japan's parliament including two cabinet ministers visited a controversial war shrine in Tokyo on Tuesday, group and shrine officials said.

It was the first visit to Yasukuni Shrine by the group, formed earlier this month in a merger of right-leaning parliament members' leagues from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) and the opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) and Taiyoto (Sun Party).
The two cabinet members among Tuesday's visitors were Transport Minister Makoto Koga and Regional Development Minister Jitsuo Inagaki, group officials said.

Yasukuni, a Shinto shrine, houses the spirits of 2.6 million Japanese who have died in wars since the 19th century, including several executed Class-A war criminals such as General Hideki Tojo, prime minister during World War Two.

Last July, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto became the first premier to visit Yasukuni in a decade, an act which immediately drew sharp criticism from China and other countries which suffered Japanese aggression in the years up to 1945.
China said such visits marked an attempt by Japan to whitewash its wartime aggression and atrocities.

"Our visit is an expression of honest prayers for peace," said Keizo Obuchi, the group's chairman and a senior LDP member, after Tuesday's visit. "There is no truth to what other people say of the visit."

Japanese Foreign Ministry officials have said Hashimoto's visit to Yasukuni last July and a festering border dispute over uninhabited islets in the South China Sea plunged Sino-Japanese ties to the lowest point since the two countries normalised relations in 1978.
Since then, however, Japan has lifted a ban on grants-in-aid to China, frozen when Beijing conducted underground nuclear tests, and has moved to mend ties.
Until the late 1970s, private visits to Yasukuni by politicians were not controversial because Tojo and other convicted war criminals were not enshrined there.
In the mid-1980s, however, priests at Yasukuni revealed they had decided to enshrine the spirits of Tojo and other executed war criminals.
Some families of the war dead protested at the move, saying the war leaders' spirits had no place among those of soldiers who had been ordered to die on the battlefield.
But others have said there should be no distinction between those who died in battle and those executed for war crimes.

The merger of the various Yasukuni legislators' leagues came at the same time that Hashimoto struck a deal with Shinshinto leader Ichiro Ozawa over a key piece of legislation over U.S. military bases on the southern island of Okinawa.
Parliament enacted the Okinawa bill last week.

Recently, there have been similar mergers of right-leaning parliament members' leagues -- some calling for closer ties with Taiwan and others demanding that history textbooks used in Japanese schools abandon an apologetic tone towards Asia.
